jsnvu6-e179456-d1e106.summary: Rubric for Question 3: whether habit contributes anything to the determination of an act, referring to Cajetan.

jsnvu6-e179456-d1e117.summary: Argument that habit determines the act: by Ethics II, power is that by which we can, habit that by which we can well or ill; good and evil are the determinations of a moral act.
claims: Habit determines the act to good or evil (objection)

jsnvu6-e179456-d1e133.summary: Second argument: an act's determination to good or bad comes either from the power or from the habit; not from the power, which is indifferent; so from the habit.
claims: Since the power is indifferent, determination must come from habit (objection)

jsnvu6-e179456-d1e147.summary: Argument for the opposite: acts preceding the habit are already determinately good or bad—good habits arise only from good acts and bad from bad—so such determination is not per se from the habit, for an effect cannot exist without its per se cause.
claims: Acts before a habit are already determinately good or bad
Hence habit is not the per se cause of an act's moral determination

jsnvu6-e179456-d1e165.summary: Key distinction: determination of a power differs from determination of an act. A power is indeterminate as a subject toward various habits or acts, and is determined formally by receiving one, with determinant and determinable really distinct as form and subject. An act's indeterminacy is only conceptual, as universal to singular; every real act is determinate in natural being by its singular existence, not by something added. Its moral determination, however, comes formally from conformity or nonconformity with right reason (as shown in Book 2). Two inquiries follow: whether habit determines the power, and whether it determines the power toward a determinate act.
claims: A power's indeterminacy is real; an act's indeterminacy is only conceptual
Every existing act is determinate in natural being by its own singularity
An act's moral goodness or badness consists formally in conformity or nonconformity with right reason

jsnvu6-e179456-d1e233.summary: First conclusion: a habit formally determines the power in itself, since any subject open to mutually incompatible forms is determined by receiving one, and rational powers can receive incompatible good and bad habits. Because habit is ordered to act, one must still ask whether it determines the power to produce a determinate act.
claims: A habit formally determines its power, excluding the incompatible contrary habit

jsnvu6-e179456-d1e259.summary: Second conclusion: habit contributes nothing to the act's determination in natural being. Such determination, being the act's real singularity, is common to all acts, before or after habit, good or bad, and so requires a common cause, which habit is not. Further, nothing can be determined toward what is common to all, and every power by nature can produce or receive only singular acts, needing nothing to determine it to singularity.
claims: Habit contributes nothing to the singular natural determination of an act
Singularity is common to every act and so needs no special determining cause
No universal act can be produced or received

jsnvu6-e179456-d1e318.summary: Third conclusion, first part: habit does not per se determine the act to moral good or evil. Moral goodness and badness are relations of conformity or nonconformity to right reason; relations are not the direct term of action but follow their foundation (Physics V); so only what per se causes the act's natural entity per se causes its goodness. Habit is not that cause, since acts preceding the habit are already determinately good or bad.
claims: Moral goodness and badness are relations of conformity to right reason
Relations are caused only through causing their foundation
Habit is not the per se cause of an act's moral determination

jsnvu6-e179456-d1e366.summary: Third conclusion, second part: habit does contribute per accidens to the moral determination, because that determination comes from the object, and habit helps present a determinate object to the power. For cognitive habits, repeated acts form a memorial disposition by which a determinate object together with its determinate middle (demonstrative or probable) is recalled with assent, so that we no longer doubt or inquire. Yet even this is not per se, since habit is neither the object nor what represents it, but a firmed custom ordering presentations. Moral habits determine the appetite through prudence acquired with them, adding that the object appears more fitting, so the appetite is more easily determined—a point about facility deferred to the next question.
claims: Moral determination of the act comes from the object
Cognitive habits are memorial dispositions recalling determinate objects and middles with assent
Habit contributes per accidens by facilitating presentation of the object, not by being or representing it
Moral habits work through prudence and by making objects appear more fitting

jsnvu6-e179456-d1e480.summary: Reply to the first argument: habit enables us to act well or ill in the ways explained—by presenting a determinate object (cognitive habits) and by making it appear as a more fitting good (moral habits).
claims: Habit makes us able to act well or ill by presenting objects and shaping their appearance

jsnvu6-e179456-d1e493.summary: Reply to the second argument: the act's determination comes neither from the power nor per se from the habit, but from the object and the middle, though per accidens from the habit as explained.
claims: The determination of the act comes from object and middle, from habit only per accidens

jsnvu6-e179456.summary: Question 3, the second of the three modes, asks whether habit contributes to the determination of the act. Against arguments that habit is what makes us act well or ill and must determine indifferent powers, Durandus notes that the acts generating a habit are already determinately good or bad. He distinguishes determination of a power (real, as form determines subject) from determination of an act (merely conceptual, as singular to universal). Three conclusions follow: (1) habit formally determines its power by excluding the incompatible contrary habit; (2) habit contributes nothing to the act's natural determination, which is simply its singular existence, common to all acts; (3) habit is not the per se cause of an act's moral goodness or badness, which are relations of conformity to right reason following on the act's entity, but it contributes per accidens by helping the object to be presented. Cognitive habits work as memorial customs recalling an object with its middle and with assent; moral habits work through prudence and by making objects appear more fitting. Determination comes properly from object and middle.
claims: Habit formally determines the power but not the act per se
An act's natural determination is its singularity, requiring no habit
Moral goodness is conformity to right reason, caused only by what causes the act's entity
Habits contribute to moral determination only per accidens by presenting objects
Cognitive habits are dispositions of memory, not representations of objects
concepts: moral goodness as conformity to right reason
